title: Knell · The sustained note
summary:
**Original lore · provisional**

The foundry strikes the unfinished core once and seals it while the metal is still ringing. Something inside takes up the note. Decades later, a mechanic can identify her old frame through a hangar wall.

Two curved iron plates hang a finger’s width apart down the back of the cockpit. At idle, the gap trembles and pale dust gathers in stripes along the plates.

I’d give it a short, wide-mouthed pulse cannon that braces against the whole forearm. When it fires, the back plates briefly touch and the note cuts out. As an enemy, that sudden silence would be your cue that the shot is coming.

items.title: Knell at idle · Front view
items.alt: Straight-on full-body portrait of Knell. Its amber optic sits above the chest hatch. The pulse cannon and upright rail unit are on the viewer’s left, with the repeater and missile cassette on the right.
items.body:
Companion to the [revised rear view](assets/knell/foundry-v002.png). The low chest hatch and narrow viewing slit interpret the side of the cockpit hidden in that study. The front angle shows the sensor head on its swivel collar, the forearm brace beneath the pulse cannon, and the left hand around the repeater grip.

items.prompt:
Use case: identity-preserve, complementary front elevation. Show the exact same KNELL mech in the reference photograph, seen by a camera that has walked around to stand directly IN FRONT OF its chassis. One full-body straight-on FRONT portrait including shoulder mounts, hands and both feet. The provided image shows the BACK. Perform a real change in viewpoint revealing the front surfaces of the chest, cockpit, hips, knees, weapons and boots. Anatomical sides are fixed; from the front they now appear on the opposite sides of the picture. The large suspended striped resonator plates and two deep booster bells belong on the BACK and are occluded by the torso from here. Keep them behind the mech. The front should unmistakably read as the front.
Identity and geometry: Broad hips, compact forward-pitched armored pilot core, small horizontal sensor head with sloping brow on the short distinct swivel collar, a single recessed amber optic visible under the brow. Clearly center the head between and above the separate lowered shoulder blocks. Infer the unseen front in the same worn industrial design: one modest, sealed low wedge-shaped armored access hatch in the chest, an understated narrow viewing slit, simple divided beveled plates with service fasteners. Keep the established graphite flexible knee sleeves, mechanical shin and heel links, broad metal toe plates, the separate small side maneuvering ports at the hips, low stable stance with both feet planted and room around the equipment. Same muted furnace umber, yellow chipped industrial paint, scale, wear and proportions as existing Knell. Broad shoulders and small head but avoid adding bulk or redesigning it as a humanoid knight.
Mount map in the OUTPUT FRONT VIEW: on IMAGE LEFT, Knell's anatomical RIGHT hand supports the same short broad flared pulse cannon with copper coil jacket, armored breech and under-slung forearm yoke; above this shoulder the same vertically stowed narrow boxy rail cannon. Aim the pulse cannon forward and slightly downward/outboard like a parked gun, so we see the flared ceramic-lined mouth plus some barrel side. Traceable bent elbow, wrist and hand under its grip. On IMAGE RIGHT, Knell's anatomical LEFT hand holds the narrower linear repeater by the grip BELOW its rear body, barrel low and slightly forward/outboard beside the thigh, fingers wrapped around grip. Above this shoulder is the same rectangular multi-cell rocket cassette. Exactly two hands, two hand weapons and these two back weapons. Keep arms a little clear of torso, both bores safely clear of booster ports. 
The original low forearm-supported carry and the shape of the sensor head matter. Keep the entire existing machine's silhouette centered, believable and distinctive in a strict frontal, chest-square-to-camera inspection portrait. Camera just below cockpit height for minimal lens distortion, long-lens natural perspective. Leave a margin around highest shoulder weapon and boots. Same cold diffuse foundry daylight, quiet distant hangar windows, subtle scale cues and worn gray concrete; grounded and sharply readable. No labels, UI, mirrored inset, split before-and-after, side figure or added effects.

items.title: Knell at idle · Revised head and weapon pose
items.alt: Rear view of Knell with a separate amber-eyed sensor head on a swivel collar. Its right forearm supports a pulse cannon facing screen right, and the left hand grips the repeater below its housing.
items.body:
**Cannon direction.** The pulse cannon follows the right forearm and the head’s sightline toward screen right. Its armored rear housing and coil jacket are visible in profile.

**Repeater grip.** The left fingers wrap around a handle beneath the housing. The barrel hangs forward and low beside the thigh.

**Sensor head.** The amber optic belongs to the rangefinder head. A short swivel collar lifts its sloping brow clear of the shoulder armor.

items.prompt:
Use case: precise-object-edit. Correct three readability mistakes in the supplied existing painting of KNELL. This is the SAME exact mech and frame, at idle in the same foundry, seen from the same rear three-quarter side: the two dusty curved resonator plates clearly identify the back. Knell's front lies AWAY from the viewer and toward the distant RIGHT side of the hall. One clean finished concept painting, full body, no annotations. Only re-pose and clarify the head and two weapon arms. Preserve the resonators, shoulder-mounted units, jets, legs, wide stance, scale cues, foundry daylight, palette and worn materials.

1. The enormous circular muzzle of the RIGHT-HAND PULSE CANNON currently faces the camera, although the viewer is behind Knell. Reverse its apparent firing direction. Swing the right forearm forward, into the depth of the hall and toward screen right, parallel to Knell's gaze and boot toes. The NEAREST end of the weapon shows a distinct armored BREECH: a closed squarish metal housing with a solid rear access plate, bolts and a short cable. From that housing the coil-wrapped barrel recedes forward to the flared ceramic muzzle at the DISTANT end. Show mostly the *outer side wall* and the lip in side/receding profile; the huge dark circular bore aiming at the viewer must disappear. Keep its characteristic short, broad flared barrel. Right gripper and forearm yoke support the breech. Bend the elbow so the cannon sits alongside the forearm rather than projecting backwards. Widen the framing slightly if needed to fit the whole weapon.

2. On SCREEN LEFT, Knell's left hand currently seems to pinch or dangle the linear repeater by its upper rail. Give it a prominent downward angled grip directly BELOW the rear housing with visible empty space above and below the gripper. Its full palm encloses that handle, three or four squared jointed fingers curling around one side, thumb closing from the other side. Align wrist with forearm, bend elbow, and bring the repeater into a natural low carry at the outside of the left thigh, with breech next to forearm and barrel pointing slightly down AND forward, away into the hall. Arrange angle so the viewer can trace left forearm -> wrist cuff -> closed hand -> underbody grip -> weapon as separate interconnected shapes. Leave the rifle's upper surface bare; no carry-loop or hand atop the barrel. Keep left hand and grip visible against the pale background. Both weapon bodies stay clear of the hips and legs.

3. The tiny sloping piece with an amber side lens near the upper right of the torso is Knell's SENSOR HEAD, distinct from the shoulder. Preserve its characteristic low sloped brow and non-human horizontal rangefinder, but lift it very slightly on a short, clearly visible dark swivel collar mounted on the forward TOP centerline of the torso. A small wedge of sky and shadow beneath its brow separates the head visually from the near shoulder armor. Keep the actual shoulder lower and outboard, a solid armor block over the arm hinge. Small head facing forward and outward to the right, away from camera, in alignment with the cannon. One amber side optic is visible to us in profile. No head on top of a shoulder, no duplicate heads, face paint, human facial features or extra weapons.

Preserve exactly two arms, two hand-held weapons, the two existing back weapons and the paired resonators down the CENTER of the back. Showcase coherent fore-aft orientation and physically readable grip. No captions, coordinate dots or diagrams.

items.title: Knell at idle · First study
items.alt: Rear three-quarter portrait of a broad-hipped mech. Two curved iron plates striped with pale dust hang above the booster bells. A wide-mouthed pulse cannon rests in a forearm yoke.
items.body:
Pale foundry dust settles into bands across the two suspended plates. The gap between them stays visible from the chase-camera side. The proposed firing cue is a moment of silence as the pulse cannon discharges and the plates touch.

The main boosters sit below the plates, with separate maneuvering nozzles in the hip armor. A forearm-braced pulse cannon and a linear repeater occupy the hands. The missile cassette and upright rail cannon flank the resonators on independent back mounts.

[Open full-resolution PNG](assets/knell/foundry-v001.png)
items.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept. A single extraordinary full-body concept painting of KNELL, a factory-built piloted eight-metre combat mech whose unfinished core was struck once and sealed while still ringing. The machine has never stopped sounding that one low note. Give its silhouette and construction a particular identity and make that sound visible through physical clues. One mech, one image, no text. 
Main view: low rear three-quarter from its weapon side, far enough around the flank to see the small sensor head in clear profile and the imposing muzzle of the cannon foreshortened to one side. The machine twists at the waist just a little, still at idle as if listening, ready to brace. The BACK OF THE COCKPIT and its two ringing plates dominate the center of the painting. Low and wide in the hips, compact forward-pitched cockpit over a narrow mechanical waist, smaller shoulders, powerful slightly bowed thighs, long calves, low plated heels. A grounded shallow crouch with the weight passing visibly into its loaded foot. Smooth black graphite sleeves flex across the knee joints to suggest the weight of living muscle. Exposed roller joints and industrial steel footplates. One bent leg can step without boost. Piloted war machine scale, not a person in a suit.
Knell's distinguishing feature: a matched pair of TALL CURVED DARK IRON RESONATOR PLATES suspended vertically down the exposed rear of the upper core. Each sweeps outward gently then curls inward like a forged spring leaf; their inner edges nearly meet down a narrow, dark, finger-width VERTICAL GAP. Tapered lower tips end well above the main exhausts. The plates hang substantially below their top suspension pins, unbolted along their lower edges so they can ring freely. They are close to the core and reach from shoulder-blade height down to the waist. A polished line on each inner edge catches oblique daylight to make the tiny air gap legible. Pale fine foundry dust shaken into several irregular but distinct parallel bands across both dark metal surfaces, a few grains drifting off an edge. Just those mechanical clues to the occult. Their shapes are paired bent sheets of iron, never wings, back weapons or a literal church bell. The head is a small horizontal rangefinder sheltered under a heavy sloping brow in profile, a tiny dull amber side optic; almost a face when it tilts. Service door and maintenance rungs on cockpit flank.
Weapons and boost: four separated detachable sci-fi mech weapons with Armored Core industrial heft. The signature NEAR HAND holds a SHORT, HUGE-MOUTHED PULSE CANNON, short dark tube with broad oval mouth and nested heat-discolored ceramic rings, dense coil jacket, the full forearm fitted into a massive supporting yoke. Aim it outward across frame so the audience can read that abruptly flared muzzle, the distinctive silhouette is short and broad. The far hand holds a narrower rectangular linear repeater low and clear of the other hip. Left and right upper rear outer hardpoints carry a low horizontal armored rocket cassette and one vertically stowed compact boxy rail cannon, carried OUTSIDE the paired resonators; no clutter across center. Two heat-darkened main booster bell nozzles low on the back just below the resonators, visible from this angle between the hip structures; a small side quick-boost nozzle recessed into either outer hip. Inactive, fluted metal skirts exposed. No jet trails or firing effects, this is the sustained note before action.
Visual family: refined original Japanese hard-surface mech industrial design, photographed-painting material realism. Muted furnace-umber, dark iron, oxidized metal, chalky gray bands, sparse old yellow maintenance paint and small rammed steel repairs. Broad planes through torso and hips with crisp, carefully concentrated machine detail in the weapons. Keep form readable and comparatively lean above the hips. Bleak empty casting hall, distant high windows and a tiny service stair for scale, softly blurred background; angled cold daylight raking across dust on plates. Full figure and equipment inside a near-square or 4:5 picture, ground contact shadows and spare margins around both feet, generous rim light for shadow separation. Not ornamental gothic fantasy: no horns, halo, robes, glowing runes, symmetrical crescent symbols, literal musical notes, sound-wave graphics, decals as captions, inset panels or HUD.

items.title: References used
items.body:
The original pitch used the shared Armored Core references for the forearm-braced cannon, independent back weapons and low booster bells. Knell’s first painting also used the round’s Gekko-like weight and flex through the legs. The pitch named no individual Pinterest pin for Knell. The paired iron plates, dust bands and sustained note came from the written concept. [Armored Core VI assembly manual](https://www.fromsoftware.jp/manual/armoredcore6/ps5/customize.html) · [Official visual gallery](https://www.armoredcore.net/gallery.html)

**Image references for the revisions**

- The [first rear study](assets/knell/foundry-v001.png) was the source for the corrected painting. The three marks on that study identified the pulse cannon’s direction, the repeater grip and the head blending into the shoulder.
- The [corrected rear study](assets/knell/foundry-v002.png) was the source for the [front view](assets/knell/front-v001.png). It established the frame, mounts and weapon orientation for the new angle.
